script: Why were the last men defending Hitler's bunker French? The Soviet flag is already over the Reichstag, half a mile from where you are standing. Your name is Henri Fenet, you are twenty-five, and the three hundred Frenchmen with you are all that is left of an SS division that once had eleven thousand men. The Red Army is two streets away, and Hitler is underground with a pistol he has not used yet. Here's the part nobody mentions. On April twenty-eighth your battalion destroys sixty-two Soviet tanks in a single day, more than any German unit still standing. The next morning they walk you into the Chancellery and pin the Knight's Cross on you. Hitler shoots himself the day after that. Your men keep fighting two more days, because nobody comes up to tell them it is over. France gives you twenty years of hard labour. You get out in 1959, live until 2002, and almost nobody ever asks. Today that bunker is a car park in Berlin with one small information board on the corner. You can go stand on the spot where the last men defending Hitler's bunker were French.

title: 300 Frenchmen Died Defending Hitler's Bunker. Why?
description:
By the last week of the war, the men holding the line around Hitler's bunker were not German. They were three hundred French volunteers, and their commander was decorated inside the Chancellery on April 29th — then sentenced to twenty years of hard labour by his own country four years later.

Today the spot is a car park in Berlin with a single information board.

Were they traitors to France, or men who picked a side and refused to leave it?
